RE: 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
(CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Dr. Oz and Dr. Keane, 
The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) appreciates the opportunity to provide 
comments on the Proposed Rule on “Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for 
Drugs,” as published in the Federal Register on April 14, 2026 (91 FR 19890). 
BCBSA is a national federation of independent, community-based and locally operated Blue 
Cross and Blue Shield companies (Plans) that collectively provide healthcare coverage for one 
in three Americans. BCBS Plans contract with 97% of hospitals and 83% of doctors across the 
country and serve those who are covered through Medicare, Medicaid, an employer, or 
purchase coverage on their own. 
BCBS Plans have a deep commitment to modernizing healthcare, including improving the 
interoperability and transparency of healthcare information. The secure and seamless flow of 
health data among patients, doctors, hospitals, and health insurance providers is essential to 
ensuring affordability and driving positive health outcomes. BCBSA and Blue Plans have been 
leaders on these issues, engaging in key initiatives to advance the access, exchange, and use 
of health data.  
BCBSA is a founding member in the Health Level 7 (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability 
Resources (FHIR) Application Programming Interface (API) standards development efforts, 
750 9th Street, NW 
Washington, DC 20001 
www.bcbs.com 
2 
 
 
 
including the HL7® Da Vinci Project, as well as the Gravity Project which is working to advance 
data standards. BCBSA has also been a longtime collaborator with the Sequoia Project. 
Individual Blue Plans are also active members across the HL7, the DaVinci Project, the 
Workgroup for Electronic Data Interchange (WEDI), and the FHIR at Scale Taskforce. Through 
these efforts, BCBSA and Plans promote alignment across the health care ecosystem and drive 
collective action towards modernizing the health care system. 
Specific to prior authorization, BCBSA and Blue Plans are committed to improving the 
experience for patients and providers, as evidenced by our 2025 prior authorization 
commitments which, in part, extends the CMS-0057 electronic prior authorization (ePA) 
technologies to the commercial market and commits Blue Plans to providing a response in near 
real time for at least 80% of electronic prior authorization requests for medical services that 
include all the necessary clinical documentation in 2027. These commitments are to ensure 
patients can get the right care, at the right place, at the right time.  
This rule is an important next step in advancing more efficient, standardized, and transparent 
prior authorization processes, specifically extending ePA to prescription drugs. To support 
successful implementation, our comments focus on technical recommendations to align CMS 
and BCBSA’s shared policy goals with the operational realities across providers, vendors and 
payers. These recommendations are intended to ensure sustainable adoption and to avoid any 
unintended disruption as we all move towards a more modernized healthcare system. Reflected 
in our detailed comments which follow, BCBSA urges CMS and ONC to take the following key 
steps: 
• 
Align implementation dates to ecosystem readiness by extending the 
implementation dates for the new APIs by two years.  Prescription drug prior 
authorization introduces substantial complexity compared to the medical ePA API – 
including variable benefit classification, cross-system coordination, and routing edge 
cases – that have not been tested end-to-end at scale. Compressing implementation 
alongside an already-active medical ePA buildout strains the same staff and technical 
resources, creating real risk of disruption to both efforts and to the patients depending on 
them. 
• 
Set clear versioning guardrails for required FHIR standards—specifically 
establishing an initial floor version and limiting implementers to only one updated version 
above the floor at a time, with a clearly defined transition mechanism and consideration 
of backward compatibility. This will ensure adoption across different stakeholders is 
mutually compatible and current.  
Encourage and support adoption of APIs across providers and EHR vendors to 
ensure full use and remove reliance on phones and faxes. The value of ePA APIs 
depends not only on technical availability, but on meaningful use by providers and 
vendors. CMS can play a critical role in promoting adoption through aligned incentives, 
clear expectations, and coordination with ongoing CMS and ONC initiatives. 
 
3 
BCBSA appreciates CMS’ and ONC’s leadership in advancing interoperability and prior 
authorization modernization and looks forward to continued collaboration to ensure these 
policies are operationally feasible, aligned across programs, and effective in improving patient 
access and care delivery. 
In what follows, we provide detailed recommendations. We appreciate your consideration of our 
comments and look forward to continued collaboration. 
We appreciate your consideration of our comments. If you have any questions or want 
additional information, please contact Jennifer Jones at Jennifer.Jones@bcbsa.com. 
Sincerely, 
Amanda Lincoln 
Vice President, Policy & Advocacy 
Blue Cross Blue Shield Association 
4 
 
 
 
 
BCBSA’S DETAILED COMMENTS ON THE INTEROPERABILITY STANDARDS AND PRIOR 
AUTHORIZATION FOR DRUGS PROPOSED RULE (CMS-0062-P) 
Issue #1: Implementation Timelines 
CMS proposes an October 1, 2027 compliance date for most provisions. 
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends that CMS extend the implementation date for the ePA 
API adoptions for prescription drugs – whether provided through medical or pharmacy – by two 
years post-finalization of the rule.    
Rationale: Beneficiaries are best served by a prior authorization system that works reliably from 
day one. A rushed implementation of prescription drug ePA APIs risks system failures, misrouted 
requests, and coverage delays that could disrupt access to critical medications. 
The proposed Oct. 1, 2027 implementation date is not feasible given the complexity of 
implementation. Successful implementation of the APIs requires real-world end-to-end testing 
and scalability, yet currently testing has only been done in limited pilot situations. It has not been 
successfully performed end-to-end, where both providers and payers would be reaching their 
back-end systems, ensuring full functionality. This testing is essential but cannot be done in little 
more than a year (assuming rapid finalization of this rule).  
Unlike the medical ePA API, prescription drug prior authorization introduces substantially greater 
complexity that, if not properly addressed, creates direct risk of coverage disruption for patients. 
Specific to medical-benefit drugs, PA is not a straightforward extension of existing capabilities. 
Unlike non-drug items and services, drug prior authorization involves more complex and 
variable benefit classification, which is not always known at the point of request and may differ 
across programs. In addition, medical-benefit drug workflows often require coordination across 
medical and pharmacy systems and rely on different data elements, including clinical and 
formulary-related information, which are not captured in existing prior authorization processes.  
Without reliable benefit routing, beneficiaries could face misrouted requests, resubmission 
requirements, or conflicting determinations – the opposite of the access improvements this rule 
intends. Plans will need to establish processes to appropriately route medical versus pharmacy 
prescription drugs to ensure efficient processing. Benefit classification is not always clear 
especially for drugs that may be billed under either the medical or pharmacy benefit depending 
on site of care, dispensing channel, or program rules. When requirements differ based on 
benefit classification, providers and plans may need to reroute requests, resubmit 
documentation, or manage parallel processes, increasing burden and the risk of rework. In 
addition, there are a subset of edge cases, such as Part B drugs dispensed through 
pharmacies, where inconsistent implementation approaches could result in duplicative or 
conflicting data across APIs and transaction standards. It will take time for plans and their 
vendors to operationalize these workflows within existing systems and business processes, 
while continuing to collaborate with industry on implementation guidance and standards 
development around these scenarios. These nuances will need to be accounted for in the 
implementation to ensure the requests can be appropriately routed and the potential for real-
time PA realized. 
5 
 
 
 
Finally, this implementation will largely lean on the same staff and technical resources that are 
focused on the medical ePA API implementation today. Aggressive timelines for the prescription 
drug implementation would strain these resources and potentially compromise the successful 
adoption of both. The medical ePA API will go live on Jan. 1, 2027 but provider and EHR 
connections and use will likely build throughout the year. While we support the expansion of ePA 
to prescription drugs, that expansion must be carefully sequenced to protect the integrity of both 
efforts and the patients they serve.   
Extending the implementation date by two years would reduce the risk of rushed or incomplete 
implementations and better position CMS to realize its long-term burden reduction goals. Plans, 
providers, Pharmacy Benefit Managers, EHR developers, and vendors will need sufficient time 
to operationalize new workflows, conduct end-to-end testing, and coordinate implementation 
across medical and pharmacy benefit prior authorization processes to ensure a seamless 
experience for beneficiaries.  
Issue #2: Scope and Definition of ePA for Drugs 
The proposed rule expands ePA requirements to drugs.  
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends that CMS clearly define how ePA requirements apply 
across medical-benefit and pharmacy-benefit drug workflows, and explicitly state that plans may 
meet these requirements through delegated entities. 
Rationale: Drug prior authorization workflows differ significantly from medical prior authorization 
workflows and often rely on distinct systems, standards, and delegated operational 
arrangements. In practice, PA intake, clinical review, and decision communication may be 
supported by different technologies and parties, particularly for pharmacy benefits. For example, 
prior authorization for a pharmacy benefit specialty drug typically flows through a pharmacy 
benefit manager’s claims and adjudication system using NCPDP SCRIPT transactions, with 
clinical review conducted by a specialty pharmacy or dedicated PA vendor. In the case of the 
same specialty drug covered under the medical benefit, the prior authorization administered in 
an infusion center, for example, would route through the health plan's utilization management 
(UM) system using FHIR-based transactions (i.e., CRD, DTR, and PAS), often reviewed by a 
separate UM contractor. 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA recommends CMS take steps to drive provider adoption of the 
ePA APIs, including: amending the Medicare Conditions of Participation to require hospitals and 
clinicians to enable FHIR-based APIs and enhancing the provider-focused Promoting 
Interoperability measure beyond demonstrating the processing of a single transaction. 
Rationale: Provider adoption is critical for determining whether expansion of the ePA APIs 
delivers meaningful operational value. When payers build and maintain compliant APIs, the 
benefits of ePA – enabling more seamless access to care for patients - cannot be realized 
without consistent provider-side enablement and use. APIs must be integrated into provider 
workflows to deliver actionable information at the point of care and minimize resubmissions. 
Policies that encourage workflow integration will help ensure electronic prior authorization 
capabilities are used consistently and provide meaningful value to providers and patients. 
6 
 
 
 
Targeted incentives, specifically updating Conditions of Participation and strengthening 
Promoting Interoperability measures, can help ensure that providers have both the technical 
capability and accountability to integrate FHIR-based prior authorization into routine workflows. 
Strengthening provider-side expectations aligns incentives across the ecosystem, promotes 
sustained use beyond minimal compliance, and helps ensure that investments in electronic prior 
authorization translate into reduced burden, faster decisions, and improved patient access to 
care.  
Issue #3 NCPDP SCRIPT Standard for Pharmacy-Benefit Drug PA 
CMS proposes to extend existing Medicare Advantage and Part D requirements to state 
Medicaid/CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and 
QHP issuers on FFEs, requiring them to support the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard for electronic PA 
of drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit by Oct. 1, 2027.  
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends requiring NCPDP SCRIPT as the single HIPAA 
standard transaction for electronic PA for retail pharmacy drugs. 
Rationale: Establishing NCPDP SCRIPT as the single HIPAA standard for electronic prior 
authorization of pharmacy-benefit drugs promotes clarity, consistency, and efficiency across the 
ecosystem. SCRIPT is a mature, pharmacy-specific standard that is already widely 
implemented for prescribing and pharmacy transactions and expanding its use for ePA builds on 
existing infrastructure and workflows. Using one dedicated standard reduces fragmentation, 
avoids parallel transaction pathways, and simplifies integration for providers, pharmacies, 
payers, and vendors. This alignment supports more predictable implementation, lowers 
administrative burden, and advances CMS’ goal of accelerating adoption of electronic prior 
authorization for the pharmacy benefit. 
Issue #4: Dependency on Delegated Entities 
The proposal does not directly account for the role of PBMs and other delegated entities in 
administering drug prior authorization. 
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends that CMS explicitly allow for ePA requirements to be 
delegated to through pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and other vendors.  
Rationale: Prior authorization functions for pharmacy-benefit drugs – as well as overall 
management of the benefit - are often administered through delegated arrangements involving 
PBMs and other vendors. Without clear recognition of these operational models, implementation 
could result in inconsistent compliance expectations, duplicative processes, or unnecessary 
complexity for entities involved in the prior authorization workflow. Clarifying that these 
requirements are not intended to upend existing delegated arrangements – similar to what CMS 
has acknowledged for delegated arrangements in other regulatory contexts - will help ensure 
that ePA requirements align with real-world pharmacy benefit workflows.  
Issue #5 Dual prior authorization workflows for medical vs. pharmacy benefit drugs  
CMS is proposing to require impacted payers to expand their existing Prior Authorization API, 
finalized in the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (89 FR 8758), to 
7 
 
 
 
incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit. CMS is also proposing to require impacted 
payers (other than MA organizations for whom requirements already exist) to support the 
proposed NCPDP standards for the ePA of drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. 
Recommendation: BCBSA supports CMS’ proposal to handle medical versus pharmacy drugs 
through separate pathways. 
Rationale: We agree that CMS’ proposal is the most sensible approach to incorporating 
prescription drugs in the context of the FHIR API implementation guides available today as well 
as the existing infrastructure around coding and claims processing differences between medical 
and pharmacy claims.  
Issue #6: Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial for Drugs 
CMS proposes that beginning October 1, 2027, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, 
Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities and QHP issuers on the federally-
facilitated exchanges be required to provide a specific reason to providers when denying a prior 
authorization request for drugs, regardless of the channel used to send the prior authorization 
request or decision (e.g., API, portal).  
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends that CMS clarify that the expectation is for payers to 
communicate the specific reason for denial through the primary channel used to communicate 
prior authorization decisions to the provider. 
Rationale: We support providing a specific reason for the denial back to the provider regardless 
of the method used to send the prior authorization request or decision. It is standard practice 
today for plans to accept prior authorizations sent by providers regardless of the channel being 
used to submit, including submission that are through electronic methods, a portal, phone, fax, 
and mail. The need for a provider to understand the denial reason is not based on the method 
used to submit the request and so should not be dependent on it.  
However, as we collectively work to move toward modernization and away from phones and 
faxes, CMS should avoid requirements which could reinforce the use of manual processes such 
as phones and faxes. This can be accomplished by clarifying that payers are able to share the 
denial reason through the primary channel it uses to communicate back to the provider for 
normal prior authorization requests, rather than leaving ambiguity around whether the original 
submission channel must be used.  
In addition, CMS does not address whether a payer that communicates a denial with a specific 
reason through one channel must also provide that same denial reason through a separate 
channel for the same transaction. This ambiguity could be interpreted to require parallel 
notifications. For example, both an electronic notification and a written notice, even where the 
provider has already received the denial reason through a complete and timely communication. 
Requiring the denial reason to be communicated through the same primary channel used to 
submit prior authorization responses would directly serve CMS' goal of ensuring providers 
receive timely, actionable information without reinforcing reliance on manual process or creating 
unnecessary duplication of efforts.  
8 
 
 
 
Issue #7: Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Non-Drug Items and Services — 
QHP Issuers on the FFEs 
CMS proposes that beginning October 1, 2027, QHP issuers on the FFEs must notify the 
requesting provider of their prior authorization decision for non-drug items and services as 
expeditiously as a patient's health condition requires, but no later than 7 calendar days after 
receiving a standard prior authorization request and no later than 72 hours after receiving an 
expedited prior authorization request. This proposal would not modify existing patient 
notification requirements under 45 CFR 147.136(b)(3), under which QHP issuers on the FFEs 
currently have up to 15 days to notify patients of a standard prior authorization decision. 
Recommendation: BCBSA supports the proposal to require QHP issuers on the FFEs to notify 
requesting providers of prior authorization decisions for non-drug items and services no later 
than 7 calendar days after receiving a standard request and no later than 72 hours after 
receiving an expedited request. 
Rationale: Extending the provider notification timeframe requirements for non-drug items and 
services to QHP issuers on the FFEs is a meaningful step toward a more consistent and 
efficient prior authorization experience for providers across all impacted payers. Providers who 
work with patients covered by multiple plan types currently face different notification timelines 
depending on the payer, which creates administrative complexity and can delay their ability to 
act on prior authorization decisions. Aligning QHP issuers on the FFE timeframes with those 
already in effect for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid 
managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities removes that disparity and supports the 
standardized, predictable processes that benefit both providers and patients.  
BCBSA also supports CMS' approach of establishing this as a new provider notification 
requirement without modifying existing patient notification timelines. Treating provider and 
patient notification as distinct obligations allows QHP issuers on the FFEs to implement the new 
provider requirement within their existing operational frameworks while preserving the consumer 
protections already in place.  
Issue #8: Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Drugs — QHP Issuers on the FFEs 
CMS proposes that beginning October 1, 2027, QHP issuers on the FFEs must notify the 
requesting provider of their prior authorization decision for any drug as expeditiously as the 
enrollee's health condition requires, but no later than 72 hours after receiving a standard prior 
authorization request and no later than 24 hours after receiving an expedited prior authorization 
request. CMS states these timeframes align with existing requirements for MA organizations for 
Part B drugs.  
Recommendation: BCBSA supports requiring QHP issuers on the FFEs to notify requesting 
providers of prior authorization decisions for drugs no later than 72 hours after receiving a 
standard request and no later than 24 hours after receiving an expedited request. 
Rationale: Establishing a drug-specific prior authorization decision timeframe for QHP issuers 
on the FFEs is an important step toward aligning provider notification requirements across 
payers. The proposed 72-hour and 24-hour timeframes are consistent with existing 
9 
 
 
 
requirements for MA organizations for Part B drugs and Part D sponsors for Part D drugs and 
reflect the general understanding that drug prior authorization decisions are typically rendered 
more quickly than prior authorization decisions for non-drug items and services. Aligning QHP 
issuers on the FFEs with these established standards creates a consistent and predictable prior 
authorization experience for providers regardless of the type of plan they are working with, 
reduces administrative variability and supports patient access to needed medications.  
Issue #9: Extension of Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes — QHP Issuers on the 
FFEs 
CMS proposes that QHP issuers on the FFEs may extend the timeframes for notifying the 
requesting provider of a prior authorization decision by up to 14 calendar days under any of the 
following circumstances: (1) the provider requests the extension; (2) the extension is justified 
and in the provider's or enrollee's interest because the QHP issuer on the FFEs needs 
additional medical evidence from another provider or the enrollee in order to issue a decision; or 
(3) the extension is justified due to extraordinary, exigent, or other non-routine circumstances 
and is in the provider's or enrollee's interest. If extended, the QHP issuer on the FFEs must 
notify the provider of its determination as expeditiously as the enrollee's health condition 
requires, but no later than upon expiration of the extension. CMS also proposes that when a 
QHP issuer on the FFEs extends the timeframe, it must notify the requesting provider in writing 
of the reasons for the extension and inform the provider of the right to file an expedited 
grievance if the provider disagrees with the decision to grant an extension. 
Recommendation: BCBSA supports the proposal to allow QHP issuers on the FFEs to extend 
prior authorization decision timeframes by up to 14 calendar days under defined circumstances. 
Rationale: The extension provision appropriately recognizes that prior authorization decisions 
for certain requests, particularly those involving incomplete clinical documentation or clinically 
complex circumstances, cannot always be rendered accurately within the baseline timeframe 
without risk of erroneous denials that ultimately harm patients physically and/or financially. 
Allowing QHP issuers to extend the timeframe when additional medical evidence is needed, 
when the provider requests an extension, or when extraordinary circumstances warrant it strikes 
a reasonable balance between the goal of timely decision-making and the clinical thoroughness 
that accurate prior authorization determinations require. A denial issued within the baseline 
timeframe on an incomplete record is not a better outcome for the patient than a well-informed 
decision rendered within an extension period on a complete record. Narrowing or eliminating the 
extension provision in the interest of speed would increase the risk of erroneous denials and the 
associated downstream appeals burden that follows. 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA recommends that CMS retain the third extension category 
permitting extensions justified by extraordinary, exigent, or other non-routine circumstances. 
Rationale: The current language appropriately recognizes that certain clinically complex prior 
authorization requests may require additional review time for reasons that do not fit neatly within 
the other extension categories. Prior authorization requests involving specialty biologics, gene 
therapies, and other high-complexity treatments often require evaluation of member-specific 
clinical circumstances, drug interaction profiles, and extensive medical necessity 
10 
 
 
 
documentation. Preserving this flexibility helps ensure that plans can conduct thorough clinical 
reviews while maintaining a framework that remains workable across the full range of drug 
categories subject to prior authorization. Removing or narrowing this provision could 
inadvertently limit the ability to appropriately review clinically complex cases and ultimately 
undermine patient access to safe and effective treatment. 
Issue #10: Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Drugs That Are Not Covered 
Outpatient Drugs 
CMS proposes that, to the extent state Medicaid and CHIP programs cover and impose prior 
authorization requirements for non-covered outpatient drugs, the prior authorization decision 
timeframe requirements applicable to non-drug items and services should apply: 7 calendar 
days for standard requests and 72 hours for expedited requests. 
Recommendation: BCBSA supports applying the non-drug prior authorization decision 
timeframes of 7 calendar days for standard requests and 72 hours for expedited requests to 
drugs falling outside the definition of "covered outpatient drug" under section 1927(k)(3) of the 
Social Security Act. 
Rationale: Drugs excluded from the definition of covered outpatient drugs under section 
1927(k)(3) of the Act are those provided as part of, or incident to, certain services for which 
payment is made as part of payment for those services rather than as direct drug 
reimbursement. Because prior authorization for these drugs is typically submitted as part of a 
bundled request covering both the drug and the associated service, applying a separate and 
shorter timeframe to the drug component would require payers to adjudicate elements of the 
same request under different standards. Aligning the timeframe for these drugs with the 
timeframe for the non-drug items and services to which they are incident eliminates that 
inconsistency and ensures that a single prior authorization decision can be rendered for the full 
scope of a bundled request within a unified timeframe. The 7-calendar-day and 72-hour 
timeframes also reflect the clinical review complexity that prior authorization requests for this 
category of drugs can involve. Drugs provided incident to services frequently require evaluation 
of clinical documentation, medical necessity criteria and member-specific context that cannot 
reliably be completed within shorter windows. 
Issue #11: Regulatory Language Clarification for Prior Authorization Decision Timeframe 
Requirements — State Medicaid and CHIP FFS Programs  
CMS proposes to revise regulatory language in 42 CFR 440.230(e) and 42 CFR 457.495(d) to 
clarify that the 7-calendar-day and 72-hour timeframes for prior authorization decisions on non-
drug items and services represent a maximum, not a minimum, and that states may establish 
shorter but not longer timeframes. CMS states these revisions do not change existing regulatory 
requirements and would be effective on the effective date of the final rule. 
Recommendation: BCBSA supports the proposal to clarify the regulatory language for state 
Medicaid FFS programs and add regulatory language for state CHIP FFS programs to explain 
that state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs must make prior authorization decisions available 
for non-drug items and services no later than 7 calendar days for standard requests and 72 
hours for expedited requests unless a shorter timeframe is established by the state.  
11 
 
 
 
Rationale: Removing the word "minimum" from 42 CFR 440.230(e) and aligning 42 CFR 
457.495(d) accordingly brings the regulatory text into conformity with CMS' stated intent, 
reduces the risk of inconsistent interpretation across states and supports the uniformity in prior 
authorization decision timeframes that the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization 
final rule was designed to achieve. 
Issue #12: Addition of Numeric Counts to Existing Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-
Drug Items and Services 
The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule requires impacted payers to 
report certain prior authorization metrics for non-drug items and services aggregated as 
percentages only. CMS proposes to also require impacted payers to report the calculated 
numerators and denominators underlying those percentage metrics. These changes would be 
effective on the effective date of the final rule and required to be reported beginning at the first 
reporting deadline following that date. 
Recommendation: BCBSA recommends that CMS not finalize the proposal to require impacted 
payers to report calculated numerators and denominators alongside existing prior authorization 
percentage metrics for non-drug items and services. 
Rationale: BCBSA supports transparency in prior authorization reporting and recognizes CMS' 
goal of ensuring that reported metrics are comprehensive and useful. However, the numeric 
count requirement does not advance that goal in a meaningful way and risks misleading public 
comparisons that could ultimately confuse patients, which the existing percentage-based 
metrics were designed to prevent. While a small percentage of denials may represent a large 
absolute number of patients, normalizing for scale is precisely the purpose of a percentage. A 
denial rate of five percent communicates the same meaningful information about a payer's 
utilization management performance regardless of whether it is derived from one thousand or 
one million prior authorization requests – and that comparability is what allows patients and the 
public to assess payer performance reliably. Raw counts, which lack that normalization, are 
highly susceptible to being taken out of context by patients, consumers and third parties as a 
standalone measure of payer performance and are more likely to produce misleading 
impressions than to improve public understanding of prior authorization practices. The 2024 
CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule finalized a percentage-based reporting 
framework after a full public comment process. That framework was designed precisely to allow 
meaningful comparison across impacted payers of different sizes and structures. Adding raw 
counts creates a parallel metric that cannot be comparably interpreted across payers and that 
third parties may use as a standalone measure of payer performance independent of the 
accompanying percentage – potentially distorting patients’ understanding of their coverage 
options.  
Finally, although CMS contends that impacted payers already possess the underlying counts as 
a byproduct of calculating the required percentages, extracting, validating, and publicly reporting 
those counts in a standardized format nonetheless imposes an incremental operational burden 
that is not justified by the marginal analytical value the counts provide to patients or 
policymakers. 
12 
 
 
 
Issue #13: New Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and Services 
CMS proposes adding six new metrics to the publicly reported prior authorization metrics for 
non-drug items and services. Four are proposed for all impacted payers: (1) total number and 
percentage of standard prior authorization requests that remain denied after appeal; (2) total 
number and percentage of expedited prior authorization requests that remain denied after 
appeal; (3) total number and percentage of standard prior authorization requests for which the 
timeframe for review was extended and the request was denied; and (4) total number and 
percentage of expedited prior authorization requests for which the timeframe for review was 
extended and the request was denied. Two additional metrics align expedited reporting with 
existing standard request reporting and are proposed for all impacted payers except state 
Medicaid FFS programs, which are not subject to expedited extension provisions under 42 CFR 
440.230: (5) total number and percentage of expedited prior authorization requests for which the 
timeframe for review was extended and the request was approved; and (6) total number and 
percentage of expedited prior authorization requests that were approved after appeal. For all 
appeal-related metrics, CMS proposes that appeals include both internal and external appeals 
at all levels, aggregated as a single metric, and that appeals not fully adjudicated within the 
reporting period may be excluded. These metrics would be effective on the effective date of the 
final rule and required to be reported beginning at the first reporting deadline following that date. 
Recommendation #1: BCBSA recommends that CMS not require reporting of the proposed 
new prior authorization metrics for non-drug items and services for the reporting period 
immediately following finalization of the final rule. 
Rationale: CMS proposes that the new metrics be effective on the effective date of the final rule 
and required at the first reporting deadline following that date. Depending on when the final rule 
is published and takes effect, the first reporting deadline could require impacted payers to report 
data for a calendar year that was already underway or completed before any obligation to 
collect the relevant data existed. This timing creates a structural implementation problem that 
would compromise the quality of the data. 
Impacted payers plan and budget for systems changes and data collection on an annual cycle. 
Requiring new metrics based on data from a calendar year that predates the final rule's 
publication does not provide a meaningful opportunity to implement the tracking and reporting 
infrastructure necessary to produce accurate results. The new metrics require systematic 
tracking of specific outcome combinations that are not captured by all plans in a standardized, 
reportable format even where underlying claims data exists. Extracting, validating and publicly 
reporting these metrics accurately requires dedicated systems work, quality assurance 
processes and vendor coordination — none of which can be planned or resourced retroactively 
for a calendar year already underway or completed.  
Reporting inaccurate data as a direct consequence of insufficient lead time would undermine 
the transparency goals CMS is seeking to advance and produce a public record that neither 
patients nor policymakers can rely on. Exempting the reporting period immediately following 
finalization would ensure that impacted payers have a full annual planning cycle to implement 
accurate and reliable reporting systems, ensuring that the data ultimately made public is 
complete, accurate and meaningfully comparable for public use. 
13 
 
 
 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA recommends that CMS not require impacted payers to report 
total number counts alongside the percentage metrics for the six proposed new prior 
authorization metrics for non-drug items and services. 
Rationale: The same concerns that apply to requiring numeric counts alongside existing prior 
authorization percentage metrics apply to the six new metrics proposed here. Percentages 
normalize for the volume of prior authorization requests, making them the more meaningful and 
reliable basis for cross-payer comparison. Raw counts lack normalization and are susceptible to 
being taken out of context by consumers and third parties as standalone measures of payer 
performance independent of the accompanying percentage. BCBSA supports the transparency 
goals that the new metrics are designed to advance and does not oppose reporting the 
percentage-based metrics themselves. However, requiring total numbers alongside those 
percentages would introduce the same risk of misleading public comparisons that BCBSA 
identifies with respect to the existing metrics, and CMS should finalize the new metrics as 
percentage-only measures consistent with the framework established in the 2024 CMS 
Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule. 
Issue #14: Scope, Reporting Deadlines and Reporting Levels for Prior Authorization 
Metrics for Drugs 
CMS proposes to require all impacted payers to annually report metrics about prior 
authorizations for drugs on their public websites, with covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs 
excluded because they are subject to existing separate reporting requirements. The scope of 
drugs is defined by payer type: for MA organizations, drugs payable under Part B that require 
prior authorization; for state Medicaid FFS programs and Medicaid managed care plans, all 
prescribed drugs described in section 1905(a)(12) of the Act that require prior authorization; for 
state CHIP FFS programs and CHIP managed care entities, all prescription drugs described in 
section 2110(a)(6) of the Act that require prior authorization; and for QHP issuers on the FFEs, 
all drugs covered by the issuer that require prior authorization.  
Reporting deadlines differ by payer type. MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS 
programs, and QHP issuers on the FFEs would be required to annually report the previous 
calendar year's metrics no later than March 31, beginning in 2028 with data from 2027. 
Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities would be required to publicly 
post the required metrics no later than 90 days after the end of their contract rating period, 
consistent with the proposed amendment to the non-drug reporting deadline in Section II.C.5 of 
this proposed rule. Reporting levels would align with those finalized in the 2024 CMS 
Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule: MA organizations at the contract level; state 
Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs at the state level; Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP 
managed care entities at the plan and program level if coverage of drugs is included in their 
contract; and QHP issuers on the FFEs at the issuer level. 
Recommendation #1: BCBSA recommends that CMS extend the drug prior authorization 
metrics compliance date by one year, requiring impacted payers to first report 2028 data by 
March 31, 2029, rather than 2027 data by March 31, 2028. 
14 
 
 
 
Rationale: Patients and policymakers are best served by drug prior authorization metrics that 
are accurate, complete, and comparable across payers – and that outcome requires adequate 
implementation time. The complexity of drug utilization management increases the risk of 
inconsistent metric application. Drug prior authorization spans multiple benefit categories — 
Part B, Part D, and commercial pharmacy benefits — each with different formulary structures, 
prior authorization trigger criteria and administrative arrangements. Many impacted payers 
delegate drug prior authorization functions to pharmacy benefit managers or other vendors, 
which introduces additional variation in how prior authorization requests are initiated, tracked 
and categorized.  
Similar complexities existed when CMS introduced prior authorization metric reporting for non-
drug items and services. In that instance, the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization 
final rule provided impacted payers approximately 25 months between publication of the final 
rule and the first reporting deadline, with the data collection period beginning nearly a full year 
after publication. The 25 months of lead time reflected CMS' recognition that first-time reporting 
requirements across multiple payer types require adequate time to build, test and validate 
reporting systems before data is made public. 
Depending on when the final rule is published, impacted payers may have significantly less time 
than CMS afforded for non-drug metrics between final rule publication and the start of the 2027 
data collection period on January 1, 2027. Impacted payers plan and budget for systems 
changes and data collection on an annual cycle and building the tracking and reporting 
infrastructure necessary to produce accurate drug metrics requires dedicated systems work, 
quality assurance processes, and vendor coordination that cannot be completed on a 
compressed timeline.  
Inaccurate or inconsistent data – a foreseeable consequence of insufficient lead time – would 
not serve patients, would not support meaningful public comparison, and would expose 
impacted payers to reputational and compliance risk for data quality issues directly linked to that 
insufficient lead time. Extending the compliance date by one year would ensure that impacted 
payers have adequate time to implement accurate and reliable reporting systems, producing 
data that patients, providers, and policymakers can actually use. 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA supports CMS’ proposal to align reporting levels for drug prior 
authorization metrics with those finalized in the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization final rule for non-drug items and services. 
Rationale: Aligning the reporting levels for drug prior authorization metrics with those already 
established for non-drug items and services promotes consistency across reporting 
requirements and builds on the infrastructure investments impacted payers have already made 
to meet existing obligations. This approach allows for meaningful comparison of drug and non-
drug prior authorization performance within and across payer types. 
Issue #15: New Prior Authorization Metrics for Drugs 
CMS proposes a set of drug prior authorization metrics to be publicly reported by each payer 
type. For MA organizations, the proposed metrics cover Part B drugs only and include, for both 
standard and expedited requests: total number and percentage approved; total number and 
15 
 
 
 
percentage denied; total number and percentage for which the timeframe for review was 
extended and the request was approved; total number and percentage for which the timeframe 
for review was extended and the request was denied; total number and percentage approved 
after appeal; total number and percentage that remain denied after appeal; and average and 
median time elapsed between submission and decision.  
For state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs and Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP 
managed care entities, the proposed metrics cover all drugs and do not differentiate between 
standard and expedited requests. These metrics include total number and percentage 
approved; total number and percentage denied; total number and percentage approved after 
appeal; total number and percentage that remain denied after appeal; and average and median 
time elapsed between submission and decision.  
For QHP issuers on the FFEs, the proposed metrics cover all drugs and mirror the full set of 
standard and expedited metrics proposed for MA organizations, applied to all drugs rather than 
Part B drugs only. 
Recommendation #1: BCBSA recommends that CMS not finalize the proposal to require 
impacted payers to report calculated numerators (the total count) and denominators alongside 
drug prior authorization percentage metrics. 
Rationale: For the same reasons BCBSA articulates with respect to the proposed numeric 
count requirement for non-drug items and services, requiring raw counts alongside percentage 
metrics for drug prior authorization does not advance shared transparency goals and risks 
confusing patients through misleading cross-payer comparisons. Percentages normalize for 
scale, enabling comparisons that empower consumers to evaluate payer performance. Drug 
prior authorization volume varies significantly across impacted payers based on factors 
unrelated to the quality of a payer's utilization management program, including membership 
size, benefit design, formulary structure, provider prescribing patterns and whether drug prior 
authorization functions are delegated to a pharmacy benefit manager. Raw counts, without the 
contextual framework necessary to account for these variables, invite inaccurate cross-payer 
comparisons by consumers and third parties. The percentage metrics proposed for drug prior 
authorization are sufficient to meet the transparency objectives of this rule and provide a more 
meaningful and comparable basis for public reporting than raw counts that cannot be interpreted 
accurately without normalization. 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA recommends CMS prioritize the development of clear, 
standardized reporting definitions, methods and implementation guidance for drug prior 
authorization metrics before the compliance date to ensure the data that is ultimately made 
public reflects payer performance accurately and can be meaningfully interpreted by the 
consumers. 
Rationale: Public reporting of drug prior authorization metrics is an important step toward 
greater transparency in how payers administer utilization management for drugs and provides 
patients, providers and regulators with meaningful information about payer performance across 
the full range of drug categories subject to prior authorization. But for these metrics to serve 
their intended purpose, the data must be sufficiently consistent and comparable across 
16 
 
 
 
impacted payers to support informed decision-making by consumers. Drug prior authorization 
spans multiple benefit categories and administrative arrangements that vary significantly across 
payer types, and BCBSA looks forward to working with CMS to ensure metric definitions are 
applied consistently across impacted payers. We encourage CMS to provide implementation 
guidance that clearly defines key terms and reporting methodologies to support consistent 
interpretation across organizations. BCBSA encourages CMS to implement both frameworks 
(drugs and non-drug items and services) in a manner that produces data that is accurate, 
consistent and meaningful to consumers across all categories of prior authorization. 
Issue #16: Modification to Required FHIR API Standards — Version-Neutral Framework  
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to conform to FHIR API standards adopted in 45 
CFR 170.215. Where more than one unexpired version of a standard is adopted in 45 
CFR170.215, impacted payers would be able to use any of the unexpired versions of the 
standard to meet the interoperability requirements. Requiring impacted payers to use an 
unexpired version of the standards adopted in the 45 CFR 170.215 automatically incorporates 
updated versions into the interoperability requirements as they are adopted by the Secretary.  
ONC also proposes updated versions of standards at 45 CFR 170.215(j)(1)-(3), (k)(1), (m), and 
(n), with a proposed January 1, 2028 expiration date for currently adopted versions. Proposed 
compliance date: October 1, 2027. 
Recommendation #1: BCBSA recommends CMS specify an initial floor version in the final rule 
along with one updated version above the floor, aligned with the versions supported by ONC.  
Rationale: Establishing clear versioning guardrails is necessary to balance standards evolution 
with operational stability. Without defined limits, a version-neutral framework risks fragmenting 
the ecosystem as providers, vendors, and partners adopt updates at different rates, significantly 
increasing complexity and cost without improving patient outcomes. Limiting the required scope 
to a baseline version - plus one updated version - provides predictability for implementers, 
supports orderly transitions as standards mature, and keeps the focus on seamless data 
exchange rather than version management. Aligning these versions with what ONC supports for 
EHR also ensures that interoperability infrastructure is consistent across stakeholders and 
therefore scalable. 
Recommendation #2: BCBSA urges CMS to establish SVAP as the mechanism for updating 
the versions post finalization of the regulatory requirements.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA); signed by Amanda Lincoln, Vice President, Policy & Advocacy.
- **Stakeholder type:** Payer; national health insurance association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Federation of independent Blue Cross and Blue Shield companies covering one in three Americans; BCBS Plans contract with 97% of hospitals and 83% of doctors; BCBSA participates in HL7 FHIR API, Da Vinci, Gravity Project, Sequoia Project, WEDI, and FHIR at Scale Taskforce efforts.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

BCBSA supports the rule's goals and many core proposals, including separate FHIR and NCPDP drug PA pathways, denial reasons, QHP timeframe alignment, endpoint reporting, API usage metrics, and FHIR-based HIPAA PA standards. It urges CMS to extend new prescription drug API implementation by two years, set FHIR versioning guardrails, clarify delegated entity/PBM compliance, drive provider and EHR adoption, avoid raw-count PA metrics, standardize reporting definitions, and clarify preemption of conflicting state requirements.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 FR 19890; 42 CFR 440.230(e); 42 CFR 457.495(d); 45 CFR 170.215; section 1927(k)(3) and 1905(a)(12) of the Social Security Act; 45 CFR 162-related HIPAA standards discussed generally.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; HL7 Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS, CDex; NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, RTPB; X12 278 and 270/271; FHIR US Core, SMART App Launch; SVAP; TEFCA; NDH IG endpoint profile.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prescription drug ePA implementation timeline**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Prescription drug PA introduces variable benefit classification, cross-system coordination, routing edge cases, and limited end-to-end testing, while relying on the same staff and technical resources implementing medical ePA.
- **Specific request:** Extend implementation dates for prescription drug ePA APIs by two years after finalization.

**Topic 2: Scope and delegated entities**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** Drug PA workflows are often split among health plans, PBMs, specialty pharmacies, vendors, and utilization-management contractors.
- **Specific request:** Clearly define applicability across medical- and pharmacy-benefit drug workflows and explicitly allow compliance through PBMs and other delegated entities.

**Topic 3: Provider adoption of ePA APIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Payer API investments will not reduce burden unless providers and EHR vendors enable and use the APIs in workflows.
- **Specific request:** Amend Medicare Conditions of Participation to require hospitals/clinicians to enable FHIR APIs and strengthen Promoting Interoperability measures beyond one transaction.

**Topic 4: NCPDP SCRIPT as pharmacy-benefit drug PA standard**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** SCRIPT is a mature pharmacy-specific standard and a single standard reduces fragmentation.
- **Specific request:** Require NCPDP SCRIPT as the single HIPAA standard transaction for electronic PA for retail pharmacy drugs.

**Topic 5: Dual medical vs pharmacy pathways**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Separate pathways reflect current FHIR API capabilities and differences in medical and pharmacy claims infrastructure.
- **Specific request:** Finalize separate FHIR-based medical-benefit and NCPDP pharmacy-benefit drug PA pathways.

**Topic 6: Denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Providers need denial reasons regardless of submission channel, but requirements should not reinforce phone/fax or require duplicative parallel notices.
- **Specific request:** Clarify payers may communicate specific denial reasons through the primary channel used for PA decisions.

**Topic 7: QHP and Medicaid/CHIP PA timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Aligning QHP provider notification timeframes reduces variability; extension flexibility prevents erroneous denials when records are incomplete or cases are complex.
- **Specific request:** Finalize 7-day/72-hour QHP non-drug timeframes, 72-hour/24-hour QHP drug timeframes, 14-day extensions under defined circumstances, and non-drug timeframes for non-covered outpatient drugs; clarify Medicaid/CHIP FFS maximum timeframes.

**Topic 8: PA metrics and reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify / Oppose in part
- **Rationale:** Percentages are normalized and comparable, while raw counts may mislead consumers and impose incremental burden. New drug metrics need sufficient lead time and standardized definitions.
- **Specific request:** Do not require raw numerators/denominators; delay new non-drug metrics for the immediately following reporting period; first require drug PA metrics for 2028 data by March 31, 2029; provide clear definitions and reporting methods.

**Topic 9: FHIR versioning and formulary information**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify / Support
- **Rationale:** A version-neutral framework can fragment the ecosystem if stakeholders adopt incompatible versions; NCPDP F&B is more appropriate for formulary information.
- **Specific request:** Set an initial floor version plus one updated version above the floor, use SVAP for future updates, account for backward compatibility, and remove drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 10: HIPAA PA standards and X12 replacement**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** X12 278 has limited adoption for PA and FHIR supports richer clinical context, better integration, and consistency with PA APIs.
- **Specific request:** Adopt FHIR-based HIPAA standards to replace X12 278 and 270/271 for PA-related authorization and coverage requirement transactions.

**Topic 11: State law and market constraints**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** State laws may prescribe different PA mechanisms or forms, creating conflicting obligations and parallel workflows.
- **Specific request:** Confirm whether federal ePA requirements preempt conflicting state requirements.

**Topic 12: API usage metrics and endpoints**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Usage metrics can show adoption, but definitions must be consistent; endpoint directories are needed for discovery and onboarding.
- **Specific request:** Define API usage metrics, successful/unsuccessful calls, PA versus step therapy/formulary exceptions/quantity limits; establish a centralized endpoint directory, standardized documentation, ownership validation, and line-of-business identification.

**Topic 13: CDex, RFIs, cybersecurity, step therapy, labs/DMEPOS, event notifications**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL/RFIs
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CDex and broader RFI topics require scope limits, realistic oversight, privacy/security harmonization, and attention to provider/vendor adoption.
- **Specific request:** Use CDex for attachments in a targeted manner; avoid certification that focuses only on payer-side compliance; align cybersecurity/interoperability rules; support resiliency, clearinghouse contingency, TEFCA use, and balanced point-to-point exchange.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S15/S21/S28:** Supports extending ePA to drugs but requests a two-year implementation extension, clear scope, delegated-entity recognition, and benefit-routing clarity.
- **S14/S19/S22/S25/S31:** Supports NCPDP SCRIPT for pharmacy-benefit drug PA and recommends it as the single HIPAA standard for retail pharmacy drugs.
- **S16/S17:** Supports denial reasons and asks CMS to clarify use of the primary response channel to avoid duplicative manual processes.
- **S20/S43:** Supports proposed QHP and Medicaid/CHIP timeframe clarifications and extension provisions, including different timeframes for drugs outside covered outpatient drug definitions.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports API usage metrics but requests clear definitions and specifications.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports centralized endpoint reporting, standardized documentation, endpoint ownership validation, and line-of-business/program identifiers.
- **S1-S3/S18/S37/S60-S65:** Requests FHIR version guardrails, SVAP as update mechanism, backward compatibility expectations, and alignment with ONC-supported versions.
- **S44-S56:** Supports adopting FHIR-based HIPAA PA standards to replace X12 for PA-related transactions and requests alignment and sequencing.
- **S66-S82:** Responds extensively to RFIs on step therapy, labs/DMEPOS, ADT/event notifications, cybersecurity, clearinghouses, TEFCA, and payer API implementation.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Extend prescription drug ePA API implementation by two years after rule finalization.
2. Define the scope of ePA for medical- and pharmacy-benefit drugs.
3. Allow plans to satisfy requirements through PBMs and delegated vendors.
4. Drive provider and EHR adoption through Conditions of Participation and stronger Promoting Interoperability measures.
5. Require NCPDP SCRIPT as the single HIPAA standard for retail pharmacy drug ePA.
6. Finalize separate FHIR and NCPDP pathways for medical- and pharmacy-benefit drugs.
7. Clarify denial reasons may be communicated through the primary response channel.
8. Finalize proposed QHP drug and non-drug timeframes and extension flexibilities.
9. Avoid reporting raw numerator/denominator counts for PA metrics.
10. Delay first drug PA metric reporting to 2028 data reported by March 31, 2029.
11. Standardize drug PA metric definitions and reporting methods.
12. Set FHIR version guardrails with an initial floor plus one updated version and SVAP updates.
13. Remove drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
14. Adopt FHIR as HIPAA standard for PA-related authorization and coverage-requirement transactions.
15. Align new requirements with existing and forthcoming CMS/ONC rulemaking.
16. Clarify federal preemption of conflicting state PA requirements.
17. Define API usage metrics and successful/unsuccessful calls.
18. Establish and maintain a centralized payer API endpoint directory with standardized documentation and validation.
19. Address cybersecurity and resilience through harmonized, risk-based approaches.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Compressed timelines; benefit classification complexity; lack of end-to-end testing; provider adoption gaps; conflicting state laws; raw count metrics; version fragmentation; uncertainty around delegated entities.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Misrouted requests, resubmissions, conflicting determinations, patient coverage delays, strain on implementation resources, misleading public comparisons, duplicative workflows, and disruption from inconsistent standards.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Limited pilots, lack of scalable end-to-end testing, shared technical staff capacity, PBM/vendor delegation structures, EHR/provider adoption, state legal constraints, reporting systems buildout, and version incompatibility.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** BCBS companies cover one in three Americans; contract with 97% of hospitals and 83% of doctors; Blue Plans commit to near-real-time responses for at least 80% of complete electronic PA requests for medical services in 2027.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Relies mainly on BCBSA/Blue Plan operational experience, HL7/Da Vinci participation, and CMS-0057 commitments.
- **Examples provided:** Part B drugs dispensed through pharmacies; specialty drugs covered under pharmacy vs medical benefit; Nebraska state PA form conflict; delegated PBM workflows; raw count metric comparison issues.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Health plans, PBMs, delegated vendors, providers, EHR vendors, patients, pharmacies, QHP issuers, Medicaid/CHIP programs, clearinghouses, regulators, and state markets.
- **Economic implications:** Rushed or duplicative requirements would increase implementation, reporting, and operational costs; clearer standards and delegated compliance reduce unnecessary burden.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible with additional time, testing, provider adoption, version guardrails, endpoint validation, and clear definitions.
- **Patient care impact:** Supports modernization but warns rushed implementation could create coverage disruptions, delays, or misrouted PA requests.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed-supportive; supportive of goals and several proposals with significant implementation modifications.
- **Tone:** Technical, collaborative, detailed.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "This rule is an important next step in advancing more efficient, standardized, and transparent prior authorization processes." - Context: Overall support.
2. "A rushed implementation of prescription drug ePA APIs risks system failures, misrouted requests, and coverage delays." - Context: Implementation timeline concern.
3. "BCBSA supports CMS’ proposal to handle medical versus pharmacy drugs through separate pathways." - Context: Dual pathway support.
4. "Establishing clear versioning guardrails is necessary to balance standards evolution with operational stability." - Context: FHIR versioning recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Central recommendation to extend drug ePA implementation by two years and delay certain metrics.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Highlights technical resource strain and reporting burden.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Supports provider adoption and workflows but warns against duplicative notices and manual processes.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Extensive cybersecurity and resilience RFI responses.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Focus on testing, scalability, benefit routing, API adoption, and endpoint validation.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Versioning guardrails, SVAP, backward compatibility, CDex, and FHIR/NCPDP maturity are core issues.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Supports reliable PA implementation to avoid coverage disruptions and delays.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Raises preemption of conflicting state requirements and HIPAA standard adoption.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Emphasizes providers, vendors, payers, PBMs, CMS, ONC, and states.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Central concern about benefit classification and separate pathways.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports endpoint directory and usage metrics while opposing misleading raw PA counts.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Addresses market-specific and resource variation, though not primarily small payer burden.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Emphasizes delegated PBM workflows, state forms, X12, clearinghouses, and PA channels.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Strong focus on vendors, EHRs, PBMs, clearinghouses, and API implementation.
